title: The basic types of sentences
summary: Every Japanese sentence is a little train: a main carriage and an engine, joined by が.

blocks.text: Picture every Japanese sentence as a small **train**. It always has two dark cars at its core: the **main carriage**, which is the thing the sentence is about, and the **engine**, which makes the sentence go and says something about the carriage. Textbooks call these the subject and the predicate.
The core of every sentence: main carriage + engine, joined by が.

The little word **が** sits on the main carriage and links it to the engine. It is the heart of Japanese grammar. Sometimes it is invisible (you will meet that in the next lesson), but it is always there.
All sentences, in any language, come down to two kinds: **A does B** and **A is B**. Japanese has three kinds of engine to say them.
The engine is a verb. In the plain form every verb ends in a **う-row sound** (う, く, す, つ, ぬ, ふ, む, る…).

The engine is a noun, so it needs help to pull the train. That help is **だ**, the copula. Think of だ as an **equals sign in a box that works one way only**: Sakura is a Japanese person, but not every Japanese person is Sakura. **です** is the polite form of だ.
A noun alone cannot pull the train: noun + だ is one engine.
An **い-adjective** (a word ending in い like 赤い) can pull the train by itself, because it already carries the meaning "is". So there is **no だ**.
The い-adjective is the whole engine.
The three engines side by side
Whatever the engine is, the main carriage in front of it takes が.

blocks.title: Three engines
rows: ends in い, no だ

blocks.title: Remember
items: An い-adjective never takes だ.
だ works one way: A = B, not B = A.

questions.note: The main carriage of a verb sentence takes が.
A noun engine needs だ to pull the train.
An い-adjective is already an engine: no だ.
降る ends in a う-row sound: a verb engine.
医者 is a noun, so it needs だ.
新しい ends in い and pulls the train by itself.
An い-adjective engine never takes だ.

questions.instruction: Which sentence is a verb sentence (A does B)?
questions.note: 歌う is a verb; the others are adjective or noun engines.

questions.instruction: Which sentence says A is B with a noun?
questions.note: A noun engine takes だ.

questions.prompt: ドアが白いだ。 is a correct sentence.
questions.note: 白い is an い-adjective, so だ cannot follow it.
questions.en: The door is white. (with an extra だ)

questions.instruction: Who or what is the main carriage?
questions.note: The word before が is the main carriage.
走る is the verb that pulls the train.
The main carriage comes before が.
暑い is an い-adjective engine.
Main carriage first, engine last.
A noun engine needs だ.
The い-adjective engine closes the sentence.

questions.instruction: Which particle follows the main carriage in 'A does B'?
questions.note: が joins the main carriage to the engine.

questions.prompt: An い-adjective needs だ to be an engine.
questions.note: い-adjectives already carry the meaning 'is'.
動物だ is a noun + だ: it pulls the train.

questions.instruction: What do textbooks call the main carriage and the engine?
questions.note: Subject = main carriage; predicate = engine.
Main carriage first, the い-adjective engine last.
